title: Watching him walk
hook: the old brahmin's pupil follows the Buddha for months, watching how he walks and eats

segments.voice: Yesterday: why the old king bows, and Pasenadi's reasons, all things he'd seen. Your line was why I bow. What real reason did you name? Day four hundred seventy-four.

How do you really get to know someone? Not their profile, not their speeches. You watch them on an ordinary day. How they treat a waiter. How they eat when they think nobody's looking. In the city of Mithilā lives a famous brahmin named Brahmāyu, a master of the old Vedic learning, and the sutta says he's a hundred and twenty years old. He hears the Buddha is nearby, and he does something careful. He sends his best student, a young man named Uttara, to watch. Not to debate. To watch.
screen: `WATCH THEM ON AN ORDINARY DAY.` → `BRAHMĀYU, A HUNDRED AND TWENTY.` → `NOT TO DEBATE. TO WATCH.`

segments.voice: Uttara follows the Buddha for seven months, the sutta says, like a shadow that never leaves. Then he goes home and reports, and his report is one of the most detailed portraits of the Buddha's body in the canon. When he walks, he steps off with the right foot. His stride is neither too long nor too short. He walks neither too fast nor too slow. His knees and ankles don't knock together. When he looks back, he turns his whole body, the way an elephant does, not just a glance over the shoulder. When he sits down in a house, he doesn't drop into the seat or fidget once he's there. When he eats, he takes neither too much rice nor too little. He chews each mouthful two or three times. He tastes the food, the report says, but without greed for the taste. After eating he sits quietly for a moment, gives thanks, and doesn't praise or criticize the meal. When he teaches, his voice is clear and carries exactly as far as the gathering, and no farther. And so it goes: robes, bowl, washing, sleeping. Notice what convinces Uttara. Not an argument. Not a wonder. A man who is the same in the kitchen as on the teaching seat. Brahmāyu hears the report, bows in the Buddha's direction, and later goes to meet him. The sutta says he understood the teaching that day and died not long after. A hundred and twenty years old, and what reached him was the description of someone eating rice.
screen: `SEVEN MONTHS, LIKE A SHADOW.` · `RIGHT FOOT FIRST, NEITHER FAST NOR SLOW.` · `TASTE WITHOUT GREED.` · `THE SAME IN THE KITCHEN AS ON THE SEAT.` · then, large: `WATCH HOW THEY WALK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch someone good for a day. Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone whose goodness you trust, not from what they say, but from how they are. Picture them doing something ordinary: walking into a room, eating, answering a phone. What do you notice? Then, for the rest of the sit, turn the same quiet attention on yourself: how you're sitting, how you're breathing, right now. The bell holds the time.
Watching him walk. Uttara followed the Buddha for seven months and reported how he walked, sat and ate. What convinced him was the ordinary. Today's word.
Your line: watch how they walk. Today, notice one good person in an ordinary moment, and eat one meal the way Uttara saw it done: tasting, without greed. Day four hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Monastic training in Buddhist traditions gives careful attention to deportment, how to walk, sit, eat and wear robes, and lay Buddhists often say they learned most from watching how a respected teacher lives day to day.

fork.setup: you're Brahmāyu, a hundred and twenty years old. you want to know if a famous teacher is the real thing. what do you do?
options: send your best student to argue with him
send your best student to watch him live
fork.reveal: Brahmāyu sends Uttara to watch. seven months of ordinary days tell him more than any debate.

original.note: Pali iriyāpatha: deportment, the postures of walking, standing, sitting and lying down.

trapdoor: what you thought: watching him walk means admiring the Buddha.
what it means: you know someone by their ordinary conduct, the same in the kitchen as on the teaching seat.

what a scholar hears: MN 91, the Brahmāyu Sutta, combines a check of the thirty-two marks of a great man with this detailed account of deportment; Brahmāyu is said to have reached non-return before he died.

notes: MN 91 paraphrased; check the deportment details (right foot first, stride, knees and ankles, the elephant look, eating, the voice) and the seven months.
The sutta's opening, on checking the thirty-two marks of a great man, is skipped for focus; the trapdoor mentions it.
Brahmāyu's age (120) and his attaining non-return and dying soon after: confirm.
